lines.text: Three whole numbers, same ratio each step.
lines.caption: Three whole numbers, same ratio each step.

lines.text: How many can finish at one hundred forty-four?
lines.caption: How many can finish at one hundred forty-four?

lines.text: How many increasing geometric sequences a, b, c of whole numbers have c equal to one hundred forty-four?
lines.caption: How many increasing geometric sequences a, b, c of whole numbers have c equal to one hundred forty-four?

lines.text: Here's the trick. One hundred forty-four is twelve squared.
lines.caption: Here's the trick. One hundred forty-four is twelve squared.

lines.text: So b over twelve must be a whole number. Call it k.
lines.caption: So b over twelve must be a whole number. Call it k.

lines.text: Then b is twelve k, and a is k squared. Try k equals one, then two, and so on!
lines.caption: Then b is twelve k, and a is k squared. Try k equals one, then two, and so on!

lines.text: At k equals twelve all three match, so we stop.
lines.caption: At k equals twelve all three match, so we stop.

lines.text: Counting k from one to eleven gives eleven sequences!
lines.caption: Counting k from one to eleven gives eleven sequences!

lines.text: Some ratios are fractions, like three halves.
lines.caption: Some ratios are fractions, like three halves.

lines.text: Why does that work? The full lesson shows two ways, plus every trap.
